title: Sovereign AI
subtitle: A summary for funders
label: Sovereign AI for funders
summary: Why the Sovereign AI program is worth funding, what the money pays for, how each pilot runs and how funders can take part.
standfirst: PL R&D's Sovereign AI program helps governments run AI on their own terms. In each country we take one public problem to a working pilot on an open model the government controls, and train the local team that will run it. We aim for three to five countries over 24 months. Funding pays for the pilots, their independent evaluation and the lessons the next country can reuse, so a government sees AI work for its priorities before it commits its own budget.

reasons.label: Why fund it
reasons.aside: Three reasons, with the evidence behind each

items.title: Governments are asking
items.promise: Capacity is the help they want first
items.text: Ministries want to choose, run and check AI themselves. Most offers they get are a product or a plan. We build the skills on a real public task.

evidence.caption: In more than 1,500 written submissions to the UN's first Global Dialogue on AI Governance, governments were the only group to rank capacity-building first. Most others put safety first.

items.title: The tools are ready
items.promise: Open models already do real public work
items.text: A government can now host and adapt an open model, such as Switzerland's Apertus, for work like translation and drafting. What most countries lack is the team to run one safely.

evidence.caption: The Canton of Ticino translates sensitive government documents on Switzerland's open model Apertus, without relying on commercial providers.

items.title: Control is at stake
items.promise: Rented AI answers to someone else
items.text: Whoever runs a government's AI shapes what its officials see. Renting all of it hands over the data, the audit trail and the choice of model. Capacity built now keeps them at home.

evidence.caption: said Microsoft France's director of public and legal affairs under oath, asked to guarantee French data would never reach US authorities without French consent. He added it had never happened yet.

funding.label: What funding pays for
funding.aside: In each country, around the government's own team

items.title: The pilot
items.text: An open model hosted where the government chooses, adapted to its languages and data, and engineers to build the service with its team.

items.title: Independent evaluation
items.text: Academic partners test models on the country's priorities and languages, then measure the pilot against the current process. We publish the results, good or bad.

items.title: A local team
items.text: Training and side-by-side work for the officials and engineers who will run and improve the system after the pilot ends.

items.title: Shared lessons
items.text: A program manager, gatherings where pilot teams compare notes, and an open playbook the next country can start from.

steps.label: How the program runs
steps.aside: In each country, from a named problem to a decision

items.title: Diagnose
items.text: Months 0 to 3. One public service or decision to improve, its owner, and a measure of success.

items.title: Design
items.text: Months 3 to 6. Data rules, oversight and red lines first, then the model and where it runs.

items.title: Pilot
items.text: Months 6 to 12. A live service used by over 1,000 people for at least 30 days, tested against the current process.

items.title: Decide and hand over
items.text: Scale, change or stop, on the evidence. The code, the know-how and the team stay with the government.

steps.bar: a measure of success agreed before work starts, results reported against it, good or bad, and open code and lessons that any country can reuse.

items.text: Fund the shared core: the first pilots, their evaluation and the program team.
Fund [a pilot](/areas/economies-governance/programs/government-pilot-partnership/) in a country or region where you already work.
Credits or hosting for open models, so each pilot runs where its government chooses.
Help a pilot that works become a national service, with the government's budget or a development bank.
Open models, open standards and open code that a government can inspect, keep and run without us.
A decade of turning research into open infrastructure used around the world: IPFS, Filecoin and libp2p.

[Broad Listening and Simocracy](/areas/economies-governance/programs/broad-listening-simocracy/), AI-assisted deliberation that has driven real budget allocations, and AI for Public Goods, a research field PL R&D co-leads, co-funded with Gitcoin.
Nearly 400 teams across Protocol Labs, and more than 22,000 researchers, builders and residents from over 80 nations in our network.

limit.title: Not every pilot will work
limit.text: Some pilots will end at the decision step, and we will publish why. One pilot does not make a country self-sufficient in AI. That takes people who stay, a budget line and years of use. The program pays for the first working system and the evidence a government needs to fund the rest.
